subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a visit is booked.
summary: The route to an appointment here is unusually well built. The telephone number is the very first thing on the page, a full-width “Book Online” bar sits directly beneath the logo, and “Schedule a Visit” appears again in the hero. A patient who has decided has three ways forward before scrolling once. The hero photograph is also real clinical work — a practitioner in gloves assessing a patient's face, not a stock portrait.

The clearest problem is that the accessibility widget sits on top of the headline. “The Complete Solution for Beauty” loses its last letters behind the button, so the largest words on the page are incomplete on a phone. Beneath that, no practitioner is named and no review appears before the decision — and the copy makes a safety claim the visitor has no way to check.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The booking mechanics here are among the strongest we have reviewed — most of what follows is about what sits around them.

scorecard.finding: A floating widget covers the end of the headline.
Real clinical imagery, but nobody named and no reviews shown.
Phone, a Book Online bar and a Schedule a Visit button, all above the fold.
Two booking actions of unequal weight, and no proof beside either.
Two floating controls sit over the content.
Phone present; no town named on the first screen.

strengthsLead: The hard part — giving a decided patient somewhere to go — is already done here, and done well.

strengths.title: The phone number is the first thing on the page.
strengths.body: 561.756.8550 sits above the logo, before anything else. For a local practice that is the correct order of priority, and most sites bury it in a footer.

strengths.title: “Book Online” is a full-width bar.
strengths.body: Impossible to miss, immediately beneath the logo, and it tells the patient the booking can be completed without a phone call. That combination is rare and valuable.

strengths.title: The hero photograph is real clinical work.
strengths.body: A practitioner in gloves assessing a patient's face. Patients distinguish this from stock photography more reliably than most practices assume, and it does real work for credibility.

strengths.title: Retail and an active social presence are both in place.
strengths.body: A shopping bag in the header indicates product sales are set up, and Instagram, Facebook and TikTok are all linked. Both are revenue and reach that many practices never build.

captionDesktop: The homepage leads with the phone number, a full-width Book Online bar and real clinical photography.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. The accessibility widget sits over the headline, cutting the end of “The Complete Solution”. A language selector floats over the copy below.

findings.heading: The accessibility widget covers the end of the headline.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 a circular accessibility control is fixed to the right of the screen, directly over the first line of the headline. “The Complete Solutio…” loses its final letters behind the button.
findings.why: The largest words on the page are incomplete. A control added to improve access is obscuring the sentence that tells a patient what the practice does — and because it is fixed, scrolling does not reveal what is behind it.
findings.recommended: Move the widget clear of the text column, or lower it so it sits beside the body copy rather than the headline. Most accessibility tools allow the anchor position to be set without any other change.

findings.heading: The practitioner in the photograph is never named.
findings.evidence: The hero shows a practitioner in gloves examining a patient. No name, qualification or supervising physician appears on the first screen, and no patient review or rating is shown.
findings.why: The photograph raises the question — who is she, and what is she qualified to do — and the page does not answer it. For injectables and energy treatments that question decides the booking, and a patient who cannot resolve it here resolves it elsewhere.
findings.recommended: Name her with her qualification beneath the hero, and place a rating with its review count beside the Schedule a Visit button.

findings.heading: The safety claim cannot be checked by the reader.
findings.evidence: The hero copy reads “We provide highly effective, reliable and safe treatments for a variety of challenging skin concerns. Each technology and treatment approach has a first-rate safety record.”
findings.why: “First-rate safety record” invites the question “according to whom” and offers no answer, so a careful reader discounts it. Claims about safety and efficacy in medical advertising are also an area where the rules vary by state and warrant professional review — that is a question for your own adviser rather than something this report can settle.
findings.recommended: Replace the claim with the evidence behind it: the devices used and their clearances, the practitioner's training, how many treatments have been performed. Specifics are both more persuasive and easier to stand behind.

findings.heading: The second booking button is quieter than the first.
findings.evidence: “Book Online” is a solid full-width blue bar. “Schedule a Visit”, lower in the hero, is white text inside a thin white outline over a photograph.
findings.why: Both do the same job, but the one placed at the moment of decision is the fainter of the two. Outlined controls over photographs are frequently read as decoration rather than as buttons.
findings.recommended: Give “Schedule a Visit” a solid fill so it carries the same weight as the bar above, or remove it and let the bar do the work alone. Two actions of equal clarity are better than two of unequal.

findings.heading: The town does not appear before the fold.
findings.evidence: The first screen carries the phone number, logo, booking bar, headline, body copy and button. Boca Raton is not named, and no address appears.
findings.why: Proximity is one of the first filters an aesthetic patient applies. A visitor arriving from a search cannot tell whether this practice is near them without hunting for it, and a proportion will not.
findings.recommended: Add the town to the headline or immediately beneath it. One word answers the question that decides whether a local patient keeps reading.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Layout follows convention cleanly — phone above, logo, menu, hero. Nothing confuses.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Excellent. A full-width booking bar is about as easy a target as a mobile screen allows.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No review, rating or credential appears beside either booking action.
A practitioner is pictured but not named, so the authority is visual rather than verifiable.
Three routes — call, book online, schedule a visit — all leading to the same place, which helps rather than confuses.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Telling the patient booking can be completed online, in the bar itself, is a genuinely helpful thing to say early.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “Highly effective, reliable and safe” with “a first-rate safety record” is four reassurances in two sentences. Notes on candidacy and downtime would be more convincing than more adjectives.

roadmap.actions: Move the accessibility widget clear of the headline. Give “Schedule a Visit” a solid fill. Add Boca Raton to the first screen.
Name the practitioner with her qualification beneath the hero. Add a rating and review count beside the booking action. Replace the safety claim with the specifics behind it.

Treatment-page depth with candidacy and downtime notes. Post-treatment review requests. Use the existing retail and social reach to bring past patients back. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: This review assessed the homepage at 390 pixels wide together with publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). Nothing in this report constitutes advertising, regulatory, medical or legal advice.
